articles.title: India's exports to US rise 11% despite tariffs, but trade deficit with China widens - MillenniumPost
articles.summary: India's exports to US rise 11% despite tariffs, but trade deficit with China widens  MillenniumPost
articles.full_text:
NEW DELHI: India's merchandise exports to the United States rose more than 11 per cent during the first six months of the current financial year despite tariff-related uncertainties, even as the country's widening trade deficit with China highlighted a growing imbalance in its commercial relations with the two economic powers.
According to the latest figures released by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, India's exports to the US increased to $50.81 billion during April-September 2026-27 from $45.73 billion in the corresponding period last year, registering growth of approximately 11.1 per cent. However, imports from the US increased at a faster pace of nearly 26 per cent, reaching $32.33 billion against $25.66 billion a year earlier. Consequently, India's merchandise trade surplus with the US narrowed to $18.48 billion from $20.07 billion during the corresponding six-month period last year. The figures indicate that bilateral trade continued to expand despite uncertainty surrounding Washington's tariff policies and ongoing negotiations for a proposed India-US trade agreement.
At the same time, China overtook the United States as India's largest trading partner during April-September, with bilateral merchandise trade reaching $91.76 billion, compared with $83.14 billion with the US. India's merchandise trade with China surged nearly 29 per cent to $91.76 billion during the first half of 2026-27, compared with $71.24 billion in the corresponding period of the previous financial year. Imports from China accounted for the overwhelming share of this trade. India imported goods worth approximately $80.35 billion from China during April-September, while exports to the neighbouring country stood at $11.41 billion. This resulted in a merchandise trade deficit of about $68.94 billion with China during the six-month period. In comparison, the trade deficit with China stood at approximately $54.48 billion during April-September 2025-26.
The widening deficit reflects the continued imbalance between India's imports from China and its exports to the country. China remains a major supplier of electronic components, industrial machinery, chemicals and other intermediate goods used by Indian manufacturers. Although Indian exports to China also recorded substantial growth, they remained significantly below the value of imports.
India's exports to China increased by approximately 36 per cent to $11.41 billion during April-September 2026-27 from $8.38 billion a year earlier. However, the increase in exports was insufficient to offset the much larger volume of imports. The data illustrate the contrasting nature of India's trade relationships with its two largest commercial partners. While India continues to maintain a merchandise trade surplus with the United States, it runs a substantial deficit with China. The US also remained India's largest individual export destination, despite China moving ahead in terms of overall bilateral trade.
India's merchandise exports to the US continued to grow despite the trade disruptions and uncertainty created by American tariff measures. The increase is significant because Indian exporters have faced concerns over their competitiveness relative to manufacturers in countries such as Vietnam, Bangladesh and Indonesia. Higher tariffs can affect the prices of Indian products in the American market, potentially influencing purchasing decisions by US importers. Nevertheless, the latest figures suggest that demand for Indian goods has remained resilient across several sectors. Electronics, engineering goods, chemicals and petroleum products have contributed to India's broader export performance. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said negotiations for the proposed India-US trade agreement were progressing in the right direction, with both sides working towards concluding the agreement at the earliest.
The first phase of the proposed agreement is nearing completion, although questions concerning tariff treatment and market access remain important elements of the negotiations. Separate figures released by China's General Administration of Customs show that India's exports to China increased 40.7 per cent to $19.26 billion during January-September 2026. However, imports from China rose 23.3 per cent to $125.19 billion during the same nine-month period, resulting in a trade deficit of $105.93 billion, up 20.7 per cent from a year earlier. The figures underline the scale of India's dependence on Chinese imports, particularly industrial inputs and manufactured goods.
Even substantial percentage increases in Indian exports have had a limited impact on the deficit because imports begin from a much larger base. For the financial year 2025-26, India's trade deficit with China stood at approximately $112.6 billion, with imports reaching $131.63 billion against exports of $19.47 billion. The latest figures suggest that the imbalance remains a significant economic challenge despite improved export performance.
Economic experts have cautioned that higher export values do not necessarily translate into proportionately greater profits or employment. Sohom Banerjee, a senior economic and AI expert, said the quality of export growth deserved as much attention as the overall figures. He pointed out that export earnings alone do not reveal how much value is generated domestically, the margins retained by Indian companies or the employment supported by additional shipments. Exporters may absorb higher costs or offer discounts to retain overseas customers, limiting the financial benefits of increased shipments. The electronics sector presents a similar challenge, as higher exports can coexist with substantial dependence on imported components. Banerjee stressed the importance of strengthening domestic manufacturing capabilities while ensuring that businesses continued to have access to essential industrial inputs. India's overall merchandise exports increased 18.51 per cent to $259.89 billion during April-September 2026-27, compared with $219.30 billion in the corresponding period last year. Merchandise imports rose to $437.53 billion from $376.17 billion, resulting in a trade deficit of $177.64 billion against $156.88 billion a year earlier.
In September alone, merchandise exports reached $44.40 billion, registering year-on-year growth of approximately 23 per cent. Imports stood at $74.61 billion, leaving a monthly merchandise trade deficit of $30.21 billion. Electronic goods emerged as a major contributor to export growth, with shipments rising 70.44 per cent to $5.31 billion in September. The broader trade figures indicate that India's export performance has strengthened despite global uncertainties, although imports have also increased substantially. The contrasting trade figures for the United States and China highlight two major priorities for India's economic policy.
With the US, the immediate challenge is maintaining export competitiveness while negotiating favourable tariff and market-access conditions. With China, the longer-term issue is reducing dependence on imported manufactured goods and expanding India's ability to supply products currently sourced from Chinese companies. Experts have emphasised the need for affordable export credit, timely tax refunds, reliable logistics and improved compliance with international product standards. At the same time, efforts to reduce dependence on Chinese imports would require stronger domestic manufacturing without disrupting industries that rely on imported machinery and components. The latest figures show that India is selling more goods to both the United States and China, but the economic outcomes remain markedly different. While trade with the US continues to generate a surplus, the expanding deficit with China remains a major concern for India's external trade position.

articles.title: EU Trade Deficit Widens to €25.2B as China Gap Grows and Machinery Trade Turns Negative - Action Forex
articles.summary: EU Trade Deficit Widens to €25.2B as China Gap Grows and Machinery Trade Turns Negative  Action Forex
articles.full_text:
The EU’s goods trade deficit widened sharply from €7.5B in August 2025 to €25.2B in August 2026, as imports grew substantially faster than exports. Extra-EU imports surged 18.2% yoy to €228.0B, outpacing the 9.4% increase in exports to €202.9B. The deterioration was also evident in the Eurozone, where the trade deficit expanded from €1.7B to €16.1B, with imports rising 16.7% against export growth of 9.9%. The weakness extended beyond a single month. During January–August, the EU shifted from a €76.4B surplus last year to a €46.1B deficit, while the Eurozone moved from a €90.9B surplus to a €5.4B deficit. Seasonally adjusted figures also confirmed a monthly deterioration, with the EU deficit widening from €5.4B in July to €12.6B in August.
China accounted for a substantial share of the EU’s worsening trade position, with the bilateral deficit widening from €30.1B to €38.4B. EU imports from China increased 19.7% yoy to €53.1B, while exports rose just 3.2% to €14.7B. The resulting €8.3B deterioration accounted for approximately 47% of the overall EU trade deficit’s annual widening. In contrast, the EU’s trade surpluses with the US and UK expanded, highlighting sharply divergent trading relationships. The surplus with the US increased from €6.3B to €8.6B, supported by 18.5% export growth, while the surplus with the UK widened from €13.1B to €15.0B as exports rose 12.1%. Meanwhile, the deficit with Norway doubled from €2.3B to €4.7B, reflecting a 38.6% increase in imports. The contrasting bilateral performances show that the deterioration was concentrated in particular trading relationships rather than uniform across major partners.
The product breakdown revealed two dominant sources of weakness: machinery and vehicles, and energy. The EU’s machinery and vehicles trade balance swung from a €7.3B surplus to a €2.5B deficit, representing a €9.8B deterioration as imports surged 23.8% yoy against export growth of just 7.7%. Meanwhile, the energy trade deficit widened from €24.3B to €31.4B, adding another €7.1B to the imbalance. Together, these categories accounted for approximately 95% of the overall annual deterioration. The broader manufactured goods surplus consequently narrowed from €14.6B to just €3.1B, although the food and drink surplus improved from €2.9B to €4.2B. August’s figures therefore highlight a trade position increasingly pressured by machinery and vehicle imports and a widening energy imbalance, alongside pronounced differences in the EU’s trading relationships with China, the US and the UK.

SUMMARY:

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title:
Brucellosis and Bovine Tuberculosis: Importation of Cattle and Bison.
OMB Control Number:
0579-0442.
( printed page 65719)
Type of Request:
Extension of approval of an information collection.
Abstract:
Under the Animal Health Protection Act (7 U.S.C. 8301et seq.) the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) of the U.S. Department of Agriculture is authorized, among other things, to prohibit or restrict the importation and interstate movement of animals and animal products to prevent the introduction into and dissemination within the United States of livestock diseases and pests. To carry out this mission, APHIS regulates the importation of animals and animal products into the United States. APHIS' Veterinary Services is the program responsible for regulating these importations.
The regulations in 9 CFR part 93 contain, among other things, provisions that address the risk that imported bovines (cattle or bison) may introduce or disseminate brucellosis or bovine tuberculosis (TB) within the United States. In 2020, APHIS amended its import regulations to establish a system to classify foreign regions at designated status levels for bovine TB and brucellosis; to establish provisions for modifying the TB or brucellosis classification of a foreign region; and establishing conditions for the importation of cattle and bison from regions with the various classifications.
TB is a contagious disease of both animals and humans. Bovine TB, caused by
Mycobacterum bovis,
can be transmitted from livestock to humans and other animals. Brucellosis is an infectious disease of animals and humans caused by the bacteria of the genus
Brucella.
The disease is characterized by abortions and impaired fertility in its principal animal hosts. Different
Brucella
species are associated with disease in different host species;
Brucella abortus
is associated with the disease in cattle and bison. There is no economically feasible treatment for brucellosis in livestock.
The activities include the request for regional classification and additional information about a region, an application for recognition of regional classification (TB and brucellosis), maintaining classification and reclassification, and the official identification and certification.
We are asking the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to approve our use of these information collection activities, as described, for an additional 3 years.
The purpose of this notice is to solicit comments from the public (as well as affected agencies) concerning our information collection. These comments will help us:
(1) Evaluate whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Agency, including whether the information will have practical utility;
(2) Evaluate the accuracy of our estimate of the burden of the collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
(3) Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
(4) Minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, through use, as appropriate, of automated, electronic, mechanical, and other collection technologies;
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of responses.
Estimate of burden:
The public burden for this collection of information is estimated to average 14.6 hours per response.
Respondents:
Foreign animal health officials; importers and exporters.
Estimated annual number of respondents:
21.
Estimated annual number of responses per respondent:
3.
Estimated annual number of responses:
62.
Estimated total annual burden on respondents:
907 hours. (Due to averaging, the total annual burden hours may not equal the product of the annual number of responses multiplied by the reporting burden per response.)
All responses to this notice will be summarized and included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will also become a matter of public record.
Done in Washington, DC, this 30th day of September 2026.
Kelly Moore,
Administrator, Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.

articles.full_text: We’d like to hear about whether you feel like the US is in a recession and what you think signals such a downturnNearly two-thirds of Americans think the US is experiencing a recession, according to a new Harris Poll conducted for the Guardian. By the typical definition of a recession – when a country’s economic growth is in the negative for two consecutive quarters – the US is not experiencing one. articles.full_text:
US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.
It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.
A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.
If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.
The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department.
Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”
News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executives Jes Staley and his links to Epstein.
Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American banker resigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan.
The Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were “indeed close” and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”.
Staley was eventually banned from the UK’s financial sector in 2023 for playing down those ties, and failed to overturn that decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year.
That included Staley admitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staff in New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchange referring to Disney princesses, in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing.
After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”.
In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”.
Barclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient.
The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”.
“This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”.
Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.”
Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.

The Draft EA evaluates the potential environmental impacts of a proposal by OA to make improvements to the granite façade of the EEOB and bring it into visual alignment with the neighboring White House. Moreover, given the EEOB's location on White House grounds, it is exempt from the requirements of the NHPA under Section 107. Nonetheless, OA is voluntarily following the NEPA and NHPA procedures for this Project because those procedures provide a generally well-understood framework for considering potential effects and receiving input from agencies, the public, and interested parties.
Purpose of and Need for the Proposed Action
The subject of the Project, the EEOB, is located to the west of the White House at 17th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue NW. The Project is proposed to rehabilitate and improve the granite façade of the EEOB to restore and beautify its physical appearance, consistent with Executive Order 14344, Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again. articles.full_text: We are advising the public that we have prepared a pest risk analysis that evaluates the risks associated with the interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi (Eutrema japonicum) for consumption from Hawaii into the continental United States. The interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi from Hawaii into the continental United States is not currently authorized. Based on the findings of the pest risk analysis, we have determined that the application of one or more designated phytosanitary measures will be sufficient to mitigate the risks of introducing or disseminating plant pests or noxious weeds via the interstate movement of fresh leaves and rhizomes of wasabi from Hawaii. We are making the pest risk analysis available to the public for review and comment.

articles.summary: The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) hereby provides notice of availability of the Emissions Value Request Process in support of the U.S. Department of the Treasury's (Treasury) and Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) administration of the section 45Z Credit for Clean Fuel Production.
articles.full_text:
AGENCY:
Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, U.S. Department of Energy.
                    ACTION:
Notice of availability.
                    SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) hereby provides notice of availability of the Emissions Value Request Process in support of the U.S. Department of the Treasury's (Treasury) and Internal Revenue Service's (IRS) administration of the section 45Z Credit for Clean Fuel Production.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: 
The Clean Fuel Production Tax Credit (Internal Revenue Code Section 45Z) was established under the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (Pub. L. 117-169), and amended by the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21). The amount of the tax credit is determined, in part, by the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions rate of the transportation fuel.
Transportation fuel producers seeking to claim the tax credit must obtain the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions rate of their transportation fuel using the applicable emissions rate table published for section 45Z, or by petitioning the Secretary of Treasury for a provisional emissions rate (PER) if the fuel's type, primary feedstock, or pathway is not included in the applicable emissions rate table. Rule 17f-2 (17 CFR 270.17f-2), entitled “Custody of Investments by Registered Management Investment Company,” was adopted in 1940 under section 17(f) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80a-17(f)) (the “Act”), and was last amended materially in 1947. Rule 17f-2 establishes safeguards for arrangements in which a registered management investment company (“fund”) is deemed to maintain custody of its own assets, such as when the fund maintains its assets in a facility that provides safekeeping but not custodial services.[1]
Form N-17f-2 (17 CFR 274.220) is entitled “Certificate of Accounting of Securities and Similar Investments in the Custody of Management Investment Companies.” Form N-17f-2 is the cover sheet for the accountant examination certificates prepared under rule 17f-2. Form N-17f-2 facilitates the filing process for accountant examination certificates. The form has a purely administrative purpose and does not require any additional information (beyond that required by rule 17f-2) to be collected. Form N-17f-2 increases the accessibility of the examination certificates to both Commission staff and interested investors by ensuring that the certificates are filed under the proper SEC file number and correct name of a fund.
The rule includes several recordkeeping or reporting requirements. The fund's directors must prepare a resolution designating not
( printed page 65817)
more than five fund officers or responsible employees who may have access to the fund's assets. The designated access persons (two or more of whom must act jointly when handling fund assets) must prepare a written notation providing certain information about each deposit or withdrawal of fund assets, and must transmit the notation to another officer or director designated by the directors. Independent public accountants must verify the fund's assets three times each year, and two of those examinations must be unscheduled.[2]
We estimate that approximately 194 funds file Form N-17f-2 each year,[3]
and that it takes approximately 2 hours per response to prepare and file Form N-17f-2 with the Commission. Commission staff further estimates that on average each fund files Form N-17f-2 approximately three times a year for a total annual hourly burden per fund of approximately 6 hours. Thus, the total annual burden for preparing and filing Form N-17f-2 is approximately 1,160 hours (an increase from the previously approved 990 hours). Commission staff estimates that it takes on average 1.25 hours of fund accountants at a cost of $243 per hour to prepare each Form N-17f-2 and 0.75 hours of clerical time at a cost of $125 per hour to file the form with the Commission for a total annual cost per fund of approximately $1,192.50. Therefore, we estimate the total cost of the hour burden for filing Form N-17f-2's collection of information requirements to be approximately $231,345.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
Under section 101(c) of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977, as amended, any mine operator or representative of miners may petition to use an alternative approach to comply with a mandatory safety standard. In response, the Secretary of Labor (Secretary) may modify the application of a mandatory safety standard to that mine if the Secretary determines that: (1) an alternative method exists that will guarantee no less protection for the miners affected than that provided by the standard; or (2) the application of the mandatory safety standard will result in a diminution of safety to the affected miners.
MSHA bases the final decision on the petitioner's statements, any comments and information submitted by interested persons, and a field investigation of the proposed equipment, system(s), and conditions at the mine. In some instances, MSHA may grant a petition for modification on the condition that the mine operator complies with other requirements noted in the decision. AGENCY:
Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, USDA.
ACTION:
Notice of availability.
SUMMARY:
We are advising the public that we have prepared a final environmental assessment and finding of no significant impact relative to permitting the field release of the insect or weevil,
Bagous nodulosus,
for the classical biological control of flowering rush (
Butomus umbellatus
L.) in the continental United States. Based on our finding of no significant impact, we have determined that an environmental impact statement need not be prepared.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ms. Kirsten Dyer, Agriculturist, Pests, Pathogens and Biocontrol Permitting, Pest Exclusion and Import Programs, PPQ, APHIS, 5601 Sunnyside Ave., Beltsville, MD 20705; (352) 554-0556; email:
Kirsten.Dyer@usda.gov.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) has prepared a final environmental assessment (EA) and finding of no significant impact (FONSI) relative to the field release of the weevil
Bagous nodulosus
Gyllenhal (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) for the classical biological control of flowering rush (
Butomus umbellatus
L.) in the continental United States. After
( printed page 65721)
completion of the environmental analysis, APHIS authorized issuance of permits for the release.
Flowering rush is an herbaceous aquatic perennial in the plant family Butomaceae. Native to Europe and Asia, flowering rush was introduced into North America by 1900, possibly both accidentally in ballast water and packing material and intentionally via the horticulture trade. It is now widely naturalized in wetlands, lakes, ditches, and slow-moving rivers in 23 States and 9 provinces surrounding the United States/Canada border and is continuing to expand outward. Flowering rush displaces native plant species, impedes water flow, alters habitat structure and nutrient cycling, damages fishing, hunting, boating, and other recreational sectors, and is difficult to control. In western North America, it provides habitat for highly damaging invasive and nuisance species.
Permitting the release of
B. nodulosus
in the continental United States is necessary to help control invasive flowering rush.
B. nodulosus,
a semi-aquatic weevil, is a highly specific and potentially very damaging biological control agent for flowering rush. Both adult and larval feeding of
B. nodulosus
have been shown to reduce the vigor of flowering rush.
B. nodulosus
attacks flowering rush very early during the field season (adults are active from April onwards) and over a long period of time (larvae can be found feeding in the plants from April to September), which should reduce the ability of the plant to compensate for the attack. Host-specificity testing indicates
B. nodulosus
is unlikely to attack non-target species.
On September 3, 2024, we published in the
Federal Register
(89 FR 71250-71251, Docket No. APHIS-2024-0032) a notice [1]
in which we announced the availability, for public review and comment, of a draft environmental assessment (EA) that examined the potential environmental impacts associated with the release of
B. nodulosus
Gyllenhal (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) in the continental United States for the biological control of flowering rush (
Butomus umbellatus
L.). Comments on the notice were required to be received on or before October 3, 2024. We received 21 comments on the EA by that date, 20 of which were in favor of the environmental release of
B. nodulosus.
One commenter was opposed to the release but did not raise substantive issues relating to the release of
B. nodulosus
into the environment. Of the 20 comments in favor of release of
B. nodulosus
into the environment, 2 commenters had additional questions related to stakeholder consultation with Canadian natural resource officials and Native American Tribes, the availability of a cost-benefit analysis, and the impacts of predation by native bird and fish populations.
We reviewed and considered the questions raised by these commenters. We have revised the final EA, where appropriate, and provided responses to the concerns expressed. Our full responses can be found in Appendix 4 of the final EA.
In this document, we are advising the public of the availability of the final EA and our finding of no significant impact (FONSI) regarding the field release of the insect,
B. nodulosus,
for biological control of flowering rush in the continental United States. Our finding, which is based on the analysis in the final EA, reflects our determination that the field release of
B. nodulosus
for the classical biological control of flowering rush in the continental United States will not have a significant impact on the quality of the human environment. Based on this finding, we have authorized permits for the field release of
B. nodulosus
for the classical biological control of flowering rush in the continental United States.

Normal reading room hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday, except holidays. Abstract:
Under the Animal Health Protection Act (7 U.S.C. 8301et seq.), the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) of the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) is authorized, among other things, to prohibit or restrict the importation and interstate movement of animals and animal products to prevent the introduction into and dissemination within the United States of livestock diseases and pests. APHIS carries out this prevention and eradication mission through the animal disease surveillance and testing carried out by its Veterinary Services (VS) program using procedures and agreements prescribed in 9 CFR part 71.
Disease prevention is the most effective method for maintaining a healthy animal population and for enhancing the United States' ability to compete in international animal and animal product trade. A key element of this approach is the restricted interstate movement of livestock within the United States to mitigate the spread of diseases, allowing APHIS to use livestock movement records to conduct disease surveillance to protect the health of livestock and poultry populations. Epidemiological data from blood and tissue sampling is used to assess the prevalence of disease and to identify its source. Coupled with animal identification, blood and tissue test results are used to trace the movement of an animal that tests positive and identify other animals it may have encountered that may also be diseased.
When a disease is suspected in a given area, sampling is used to determine its presence or absence and to estimate the incidence or prevalence if it is present. The amount of sampling may increase in selected areas when a disease outbreak is suspected, then reduced in that area when sufficient tests have been done to prove the suspicion was unfounded or, if found, after the disease is eradicated. Sampling is also used to provide data for new or updated risk analyses in support of disease control programs, and, as required, opening international markets for animal products.
Regulations at 9 CFR 71.20 and 71.21 authorize APHIS to conduct disease surveillance and blood and tissue sampling activities using Livestock Facility Agreements and Listing Agreements between APHIS and owners and operators of slaughtering and rendering establishments and livestock marketing facilities. APHIS requires all livestock facilities that enter into Approval of Livestock Facility Agreements (which are voluntary) to agree to inspection, and to record animal identification, make timely notifications, and take other actions that facilitate tracking animal movements and identifying possible disease occurrences. APHIS requires all slaughtering and rendering establishments that receive livestock or poultry interstate to enter Listing Agreements that permit the Agency to conduct blood and tissue sampling at the facilities. The Agreements are critical during disease outbreaks as they reduce delays in assessments and, subsequently, disease spread. Facilities must agree to inspection and compliance reviews. Denial or involuntary withdrawal from a facility or listing agreement may be appealed. Other information activities include providing schedules of sale days, posting of quarantine signs, and maintaining certain records.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites the general public to take this opportunity to comment on an extension, without change, of a currently approved information collection. In accordance with the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, this notice seeks comments concerning the Tribal Homeland Security Grant Program (THSGP) investment justification, which allows Indian Tribes to apply for Federal Funding to support efforts to achieve target capabilities related to preventing, preparing for, protecting against, or responding to acts of terrorism.

The THSGP's allowable costs support efforts of Tribes to build and sustain core capabilities to prepare for, prevent, protect against, and respond to acts of terrorism. The THSGP also plays an important role in the implementation of the National Preparedness System by supporting the building, sustainment, and delivery of core capabilities essential to achieving FEMA's National Preparedness Goal of a secure and resilient Nation. Federally recognized Tribes are those Tribes appearing on the list published by the Secretary of the Interior pursuant to the Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List Act of 1994 (Pub. The National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), Alaska Regional Office, is requesting an extension of a currently approved information collection that contains applications for permits and transfers necessary for NMFS to manage the Amendment 80 Program (A80 Program).
Under the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act 16 U.S.C. 1801et seq.,
the Secretary of Commerce is responsible for the conservation and management of marine fishery resources within the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) of the United States through NOAA/NMFS. NMFS Alaska Region manages the EEZ off Alaska under the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands Management Area (BSAI FMP) and the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Gulf of Alaska. The North Pacific Fishery Management Council recommended A80 to the BSAI FMP in June 2006 (72 FR 52668, September 14, 2007). A80 allocates several Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands (BSAI) non-pollock trawl groundfish species among trawl fishery sectors, established a limited access privilege program (LAPP), and facilitated the formation of harvesting cooperatives in the non-American Fisheries Act (non-AFA) trawl catcher/processor sector. More
( printed page 65732)
information on the A80 Program is provided on the NMFS Alaska Region website at
https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/alaska/sustainable-fisheries/bering-sea-and-aleutian-islands-amendment-80-groundfish-trawl-fishery.
This collection contains applications used by: (1) an individual or business entity to apply for A80 quota share, (2) A80 quota shareholders to transfer A80 quota share and to apply for an A80 limited access fishery permit, (3) A80 cooperatives to apply for cooperative quota and transfer cooperative quota, (4) cooperatives or Community Development Quota groups to exchange community quota for one eligible flatfish species with community quota of a different eligible flatfish species, and (5) A80 vessel owners to replace their vessels. This information collection also contains the appeals process for an application that is denied.
The type of information collected includes information on the applicants, transferors, transferees, permits, vessels, quota share, cooperative quota, and flatfish harvest quota.
NMFS uses this information to establish eligibility to receive A80 quota share, cooperative quota, and permits; transfer and assign harvest quota; replace vessels used in the A80 Program; determine A80 species initial total allowable catch assignments; determine which vessels must be tracked for catch accounting; and review ownership and control information to ensure that quota share and cooperative quota use caps are not exceeded.

On occasion, annually.

Required to Obtain or Retain Benefits.

Needs and Uses:
The Office of International Affairs, Trade, and Commerce of the National Marine Fisheries Service requests renewal of an existing information collection.
The 1982 Convention on the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (the Convention) established the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) for the purpose of protecting and conserving the marine living resources in the waters surrounding Antarctica. The Convention is based upon an ecosystem approach to the conservation of marine living resources and incorporates standards designed to ensure the conservation of individual populations and species and the Antarctic marine ecosystem.
The United States (U.S.) is a Contracting Party to the Convention and a member of CCAMLR and the Scientific Committee established by the Convention.
On November 8, 1984, the President signed Public Law 98-623, the Antarctic Marine Living Resources Convention Act (AMLRCA, or the Act). The Act directs and authorizes the U.S. to take actions necessary to meet its treaty obligations as a Contracting Party to the
( printed page 65730)
Convention. The regulations implementing AMLRCA are at 50 CFR part 300, subpart G. The record keeping and reporting requirements at 50 CFR part 300 form the basis for this collection of information. This collection of information concerns CCAMLR Ecosystem Monitoring Program (CEMP) activities, scientific research in the Convention Area, U.S. vessel permit applicants and/or harvesting vessel operators, and U.S. importers, exporters, and re-exporters of Antarctic marine living resources (AMLR).

Members of CCAMLR are required to provide, in a manner and at such intervals as may be prescribed, information about harvesting activities, including fishing areas and vessels, so as to enable reliable catch and effort statistics to be compiled.

The staff of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) will prepare an environmental impact statement (EIS) that will discuss the environmental impacts of the Texas Gateway Project involving construction and operation of facilities by Gulf South Pipeline Company, LLC (Gulf South) in Panola, Shelby, San Augustine, Sabine, Jasper, Newton, and San Jacinto counties, Texas and Beauregard Parish, Louisiana. The Commission will use this EIS in its decision-making process to determine whether the project is in the public convenience and necessity.
As part of the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review process, the Commission takes into account concerns the public may have about proposals and the environmental impacts that could result from its action whenever it considers the issuance of a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity. This gathering of public input is referred to as “scoping.” The main goal of the scoping process is to focus the analysis in the environmental document on the important environmental issues. On August 25, 2026, the Commission issued a
Notice of Intent to Prepare an Environmental Impact Statement for the Proposed Texas Gateway Project, Request for Comments on Environmental Issues, and Schedule for Environmental Review
(NOI). Through the NOI, the Commission initiated an initial public scoping period and requested comments on the scope of environmental issues to be addressed in the EIS. With this current Notice, the Commission is announcing an additional scoping period, which will also allow interested stakeholders an opportunity to participate in in-person scoping sessions. Comments received during the previous and current scoping periods will be considered in the Commission staff's environmental review and in the development of the EIS. Additional information about the Commission's NEPA process is described below in the
NEPA Process and Environmental Document
section of this notice.
By this notice, the Commission requests public comments on the scope of issues to address in the EIS. To ensure that your comments are timely and properly recorded, please submit your comments so that the Commission receives them in Washington, DC on or before 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on November 12, 2026. Comments may be submitted in written or oral form. Further details on how to submit comments are provided in the
Public Participation
section of this notice.
Your comments should focus on the potential environmental effects, reasonable alternatives, and measures to avoid or lessen environmental impacts. Your input will help the Commission staff determine what issues they need to evaluate in the EIS. Commission staff will consider all written or oral comments during the preparation of the EIS.
If you submitted comments on this project to the Commission before the opening of this docket on June 26, 2026, you will need to file those comments in Docket No. CP26-547-000 to ensure they are considered as part of this proceeding.
This notice is being sent to the Commission's current environmental mailing list for this project. State and local government representatives should notify their constituents of this proposed project and encourage them to comment on their areas of concern.
If you are a landowner receiving this notice, a pipeline company representative may contact you about the acquisition of an easement to construct, operate, and maintain the proposed facilities. The company would seek to negotiate a mutually acceptable easement agreement. You are not required to enter into an agreement. However, if the Commission approves the project, the Natural Gas Act conveys the right of eminent domain to the company. Therefore, if you and the company do not reach an easement agreement, the pipeline company could initiate condemnation proceedings in court. In such instances, compensation would be determined by a judge in accordance with state law. The Commission does not subsequently grant, exercise, or oversee the exercise of that eminent domain authority. The courts have exclusive authority to handle eminent domain cases; the Commission has no jurisdiction over these matters.
Gulf South provided landowners with a fact sheet prepared by the FERC entitled “An Interstate Natural Gas Facility On My Land? What Do I Need To Know?” which addresses typically asked questions, including the use of eminent domain and how to participate in the Commission's proceedings. This

fact sheet along with other landowner topics of interest are available for viewing on the FERC website (
www.ferc.gov) under the Natural Gas, Landowner Topics link.

www.ferc.gov) under the link to FERC Online. With eFiling, you can provide comments in a variety of formats by attaching them as a file with your submission. New eFiling users must first create an account by clicking on “eRegister.” You will be asked to select the type of filing you are making; a comment on a particular project is considered a “Comment on a Filing”;

AGENCY:

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) intends to request that the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) extend approval, with modifications, under the Paperwork Reduction Act, of a collection of information contained in PBGC's regulation on special financial assistance (SFA). The purpose of the information collection is to gather information necessary for PBGC to operate this special financial assistance program. PBGC is also proposing changes to the information collected with the Annual Statement of Compliance (ASOC) by adding requests for filers to provide documentation regarding plan investment policies and procedures for locating missing participants. This notice informs the public of PBGC's intent and solicits public comment on the collection of information.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 15, 2026, to be assured of consideration.
ADDRESSES:
Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal: http://www.regulations.gov.
Follow the online instructions for submitting comments.
Mail or Hand Delivery:
Regulatory Affairs Division, Office of the General Counsel, Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, 445 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024-2101.
Commenters are strongly encouraged to submit comments electronically. Commenters who submit comments on paper by mail should allow sufficient time for mailed comments to be received before the close of the comment period.
All submissions received must include the agency's name (Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, or PBGC) and refer to OMB control number 1212-0074. All comments received will be posted without change to PBGC's website,
www.pbgc.gov,
including any personal information provided. Do not submit comments that include any personally identifiable information (such as name, address, or other contact information) or confidential business information that you do not want publicly disclosed. Comments may be submitted anonymously.
Copies of the collection of information may be obtained by writing to Disclosure Division (
disclosure@pbgc.gov), Office of the General Counsel, Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, 445 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024-2101, or calling 202-229-4040 during normal business hours. Part 4262 of PBGC's regulations, “Special Financial Assistance by PBGC,” provides guidance to multiemployer pension plan sponsors on eligibility, determining the amount of SFA, content of an application for SFA, the process of applying, PBGC's review of applications, restrictions and conditions, and reporting and notice requirements.
Under § 4262.16(i), a plan sponsor of a plan that has received SFA must file an Annual Statement of Compliance (ASOC) with the restrictions and conditions under section 4262 of ERISA and part 4262 once every year through 2051. PBGC needs the information in the ASOC to ensure that a plan is compliant with SFA restrictions and conditions. The current ASOC instructions require, among other documents, audited financial statements, actuarial valuation reports, account statements demonstrating segregation of SFA funds, investment/custodian account statements, SFA investment allocation worksheets, zone certifications, and updated cash-flow projections. The current instructions also state that PBGC may request additional documents and information as needed for the plan to demonstrate

compliance with the restrictions and conditions.

Specifically, PBGC is proposing to require plans to submit the plan's most recent investment policy statement, investment guidelines, asset allocation policy, investment committee charter, or other written policy or governing document, if any, used by the plan's board of trustees, investment committee, or other fiduciary committee to guide, monitor, or evaluate the investment of plan assets, including SFA assets. AGENCY:
Office of Refugee Resettlement, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Request for public comments.
SUMMARY:
The Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR) is requesting a three-year extension with revisions of the Unaccompanied Refugee Minors (URM) Program ORR-3 Report and ORR-4 Report (Office of Management and Budget #0970-0034, expiration 11/30/2026). Revisions were made to reduce burden and streamline information collection.
Description:
The ORR-3 Report is submitted to report a youth's initial placement in the URM Program, termination from the program, or re-entry into the program. The ORR-3 is also submitted to report changes to the youth's case (
e.g.,
change in legal responsibility, change in foster home placement, etc.). The ORR-4 Report is submitted annually and at termination to report on the youth's receipt of services and outcomes. Proposed revisions to the forms include replacing multiple follow-up outcome reports with a single termination outcome report, replacing self-reported outcome measures from youth with provider-reported measures, eliminating select sub-types of ORR-3 reports, replacing or streamlining unclear questions and response options, removing unnecessary questions, and streamlining supplemental report instructions to integrate more guidance directly into the forms.
Respondents:
URM state/replacement designee agencies and URM provider agencies.
Annual Burden Estimates
The edits described above will result in a reduction in annual burden estimates of approximately 41 percent once implemented. Additionally, youth have been removed as a respondent to the ORR-4 Report; youth outcome measures will no longer be self-reported, instead providers will report youth outcomes. Revisions will be implemented after a 12-month implementation timeframe; the following burden estimates are specific to the revised versions following the 12-month implementation period.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
ACTION:
Temporary rule; reallocation.
SUMMARY:
NMFS is reallocating the projected unused amount of the 2026 Atka mackerel incidental catch allowance (ICA) for the Bering Sea subarea and Eastern Aleutian district (BS/EAI) to the Amendment 80 cooperative allocation for the BS/EAI in the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands management area (BSAI). This action is necessary to allow the 2026 total allowable catch (TAC) of Atka mackerel in the BS/EAI to be fully harvested.
DATES:
Effective October 16, 2026 through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Steve Whitney, 907-586-7228.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the
( printed page 65695)
BSAI according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands Management Area (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of 50 CFR part 600 and 50 CFR part 679.
The 2026 Atka mackerel ICA for the BSAI trawl limited access sector and the non-trawl gear sector for the BS/EAI is 800 metric tons (mt) and the 2026 Atka mackerel TAC allocated to the Amendment 80 sector for the BS/EAI is 32,819 mt as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the BSAI (91 FR 11750, March 10, 2026). For 2026, all Amendment 80 vessels are part of the sole Amendment 80 cooperative, so the TAC allocated to the Amendment 80 sector is allocated entirely to the sole Amendment 80 cooperative and no TAC is assigned to the Amendment 80 limited access fishery.
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS has determined that 700 mt of the Atka mackerel ICA for the BS/EAI will not be harvested. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.91(f), NMFS reallocates 700 mt of Atka mackerel from the BS/EAI ICA to the BS/EAI Amendment 80 cooperative allocation in the BS/EAI. In accordance with § 679.91(f), NMFS will reissue the cooperative quota permit for the reallocated Atka mackerel following the procedures set forth in § 679.91(f)(3).
The harvest specifications for Atka mackerel included in the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish in the BSAI (91 FR 11750, March 10, 2026) are revised as follows: 100 mt of Atka mackerel for the BS/EAI ICA and 33,519 mt of Atka mackerel for the Amendment 80 cooperative allocation for the BS/EAI. AGENCY:
National Park Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The National Park Service (NPS) amends special regulations for Denali National Park and Preserve to conform the regulations regarding the number of vehicles that can travel on the restricted section of the Denali Park Road (miles 15-90) to a Vehicle Management Plan that the NPS has been implementing since 2012. This rule implements the plan's limit that no more than 160 vehicles may travel on the restricted section of the road per 24-hour period during the visitor season (also referred to as the “allocation season”), defined in the park's General Management Plan as beginning on the Saturday before Memorial Day and ending on the second Thursday after Labor Day. This limit allows the NPS to meet growing visitor demand while maintaining a high-quality experience for visitors.
DATES:
This rule is effective November 16, 2026.

Denali Park Road and Vehicle Management Plan
In 1917, Congress established Mount McKinley National Park as a “game refuge” with the intent that it be “set apart as a public park for the benefit and enjoyment of the people” (39 Stat.

In 1980, Congress passed the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA, Pub.

A general purpose of all ANILCA lands is to preserve them for the benefit, use, education and inspiration of present and future generations.

The Denali Park Road (“park road”) serves both of these purposes.
Built over 16 years (1922-1938), the historic 92-mile park road is an important means of access to the park and is one of the best places in the world for the public to observe large northern mammals in their natural habitat.
Visitors traveling the park road often observe Dall sheep, caribou, wolves, grizzly bears, moose, and foxes.
Nowhere else in America can visitors observe such concentrations of these large species of wildlife in such an accessible natural setting.
Visitors traveling the road also have many opportunities to observe smaller mammals and birds, some of which are rarely seen elsewhere in North America.
Alaska Range features, such as glacially carved mountains, Mount McKinley, and the open views of dynamic alpine landscapes, also are a source of visitor enjoyment and inspiration.
The park road facilitates wilderness recreational opportunities and supports freedom of discovery, a sense of adventure, and a connection to nature.

The NPS's ability to balance the protection of park resources while offering quality visitor experiences is exemplified in the management of the park road. Road crews use graders and haul gravel to maintain it, rangers patrol it, and commercial services staff manage the transportation concession contract for it, so visitors can ride buses to view wildlife and access the park's wilderness. In 2012, planning staff, with

public input, worked to create the Denali Park Road Vehicle Management Plan and Environmental Impact Statement (VMP), which adopted an adaptive management strategy that includes measurable indicators and standards for visitor experience and resource protection.[1]
These include crowding standards for the number of vehicles at wildlife stops, in a viewscape, and at a rest area; the spacing of vehicles to ensure time for sheep crossings; restrictions to night-time traffic volumes; and restrictions to large (construction-related) vehicle traffic. On September 27, 2012, the Regional Director, Alaska signed a Record of Decision (ROD) selecting the preferred alternative in the VMP for implementation. One standard in the selected alternative limits the maximum level of vehicle use on the restricted section of the park road (miles 15-90) to 160 vehicles per 24-hour period in the visitor season, defined in the park's General Management Plan (GMP) as the season beginning on the Saturday before Memorial Day and ending on the second Thursday after Labor Day. This standard allows the NPS to meet growing visitor demand while maintaining a high-quality experience. The NPS has been managing vehicle use on the park road consistent with the VMP since 2012. Resources staff monitor this and other indicators in the VMP to ensure the road is managed according to the plan.

This rule conforms the park's special regulations to reflect how the NPS has managed the park road since adoption of the VMP in 2012.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce.
                    ACTION:
Temporary rule; closure.
                    SUMMARY:
NMFS is prohibiting retention of shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the Gulf of Alaska (GOA) except by catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit. This action is necessary because the 2026 shortraker rockfish total allowable catch (TAC) in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA for vessels other than Central GOA Rockfish Program catcher/processors will soon be or has been reached.
                    DATES:
Effective 1200 hours, Alaska local time (A.l.t.), October 14, 2026, through 2400 hours, A.l.t., December 31, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
NMFS manages the groundfish fishery in the GOA exclusive economic zone according to the Fishery Management Plan for Groundfish of the GOA (FMP) prepared and recommended by the North Pacific Fishery Management Council under authority of the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act (Magnuson-Stevens Act). Regulations governing fishing by U.S. vessels in accordance with the FMP appear at subpart H of 50 CFR part 600 and 50 CFR part 679.
The 2026 shortraker rockfish TAC in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA for vessels other than catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit is 113 metric tons as established by the final 2026 and 2027 harvest specifications for groundfish of the GOA (91 FR 11902, March 11, 2026).
The Regional Administrator, Alaska Region, NMFS has determined that the 2026 TAC of shortraker rockfish for vessels other than catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit will soon be or has been reached. Therefore, in accordance with § 679.20(d)(2), NMFS is prohibiting retention of shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA and requiring that shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA be treated in the same manner as a prohibited species, as described under § 679.21(a)(2), for the remainder of the year, except for shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA caught by catcher vessels using hook-and-line, pot, or jig gear as described in § 679.20(j) or caught by catcher vessels using trawl gear participating in the electronic monitoring program as described in § 679.21(a)(2). This action is necessary to prevent exceeding the 2026 shortraker rockfish TAC in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA. This action does not apply to catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit. While this prohibition is effective the requirements of § 679.20(j)(4) apply.
Classification
NMFS issues this action pursuant to section 305(d) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act. This action is required by 50 CFR part 679, which was issued pursuant to section 304(b) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, and is exempt from review under Executive Order 12866.
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), there is good cause to waive prior notice and an opportunity for public comment on this action, as notice and comment would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest, as it would prevent NMFS from responding to the most recent fisheries data in a timely fashion and would delay prohibiting the retention of shortraker rockfish for vessels other than catcher/processors checked-in to the Central GOA Rockfish Program who are fishing with a rockfish cooperative quota permit. NMFS was unable to publish a notice providing time for public comment because the most recent, relevant data on the total catch of shortraker rockfish in the Central Regulatory Area of the GOA only became available as of October 13, 2026.
There is good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) to establish an effective date less than 30 days after date of publication. This finding is based upon the reasons provided above for waiver of prior notice and opportunity for public comment.

The requirement in 46 CFR 10.403(a)(7) to electronically submit mariner course completion data will not be implemented before November 25, 2028.
                    FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
                        For information about this document, call or email Mr. Brian T. Eichelberger, Office of Merchant Mariner Credentialing, Coast Guard; telephone 571-608-2071, email 
                        Brian.T.Eichelberger@uscg.mil.
                    
Background and Discussion
                        The Coast Guard issues Merchant Mariner Credentials to mariners who have met the regulatory requirements for individual endorsement(s), as described in 46 CFR parts 10, 11, 12, and 13. The general standards for Coast Guard-approved courses and programs are found in 46 CFR 10.403. On November 25, 2024, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Coast Guard, issued a final rule titled “Electronic Submission of Mariner Course Completion Data” [] 
                        
                         hereafter, “2024 final rule.”
                    
The 2024 final rule amended 46 CFR 10.403 to require Coast Guard-approved training providers to electronically submit the mariner course completion data listed in 46 CFR 10.403(b)(7)(i) through (v) to the National Maritime Center within 5 business days after a student completes a Coast Guard-approved course or program. The 2024 final rule stated Coast Guard-approved training providers were required to comply with this regulation by November 25, 2026.
At the time the 2024 final rule was published, the Coast Guard anticipated using the Homeport online portal as the mechanism for the electronic submission of course completion data, pending development of an updated information technology system. However, on April 12, 2025, the Coast Guard decommissioned the Homeport online portal because of increased operating costs, system obsolescence, and cybersecurity concerns.
                        On September 14, 2026, the Coast Guard announced the initial release of NavitaTM
                        , a new digital platform designed to streamline the application and issuance of merchant mariner credentials.[] 
                        
                         NavitaTM
                         is intended to replace the current labor-intensive manual mariner credentialing process.
                    
                        NavitaTM
                         will include a dedicated mariner training provider module that will facilitate electronic submission of mariner course completion data as required by 46 CFR 10.403(b)(7). The Coast Guard expects the NavitaTM
                         mariner training provider module to become fully operational in January 2028. Accordingly, the Coast Guard expects to begin the requirement for electronic submission of mariner course completion data on November 25, 2028.
                    
                        Before requiring the electronic submission of course completion data, the Coast Guard will notify the public through publication in the 
                        Federal Register
                         announcing the availability of the NavitaTM
                         mariner training provider capability and will provide guidance to facilitate meeting the requirements for electronic submission. In the interim, mariners should continue to submit their course completion certificates to the National Maritime Center with their merchant mariner credential applications.
                    
This notice is issued under authority of 5 U.S.C. 552(a).
                        R.C. Compher,
Rear Admiral, U.S. Coast Guard, Assistant Commandant for Prevention Policy.

AGENCY:

ACTION:

SUMMARY:
This action establishes Class E airspace at Ranch at Double Gates Airport, Coleman, TX. This action supports new instrument procedures and instrument flight rule (IFR) operations.
DATES:
Effective 0901 UTC, December 24, 2026. The Director of the Federal Register approves this incorporation by reference action under 1 CFR part 51, subject to the annual revision of FAA Order JO 7400.11 and publication of conforming amendments.

using the FAA Docket number. Electronic retrieval help and guidelines are available on the website. It is available 24 hours each day, 365 days each year. An electronic copy of this document may also be downloaded from

www.faa.gov/air_traffic/publications/. You may also contact the Rules and Regulations Group, Office of Policy, Federal Aviation Administration, 800 Independence Avenue SW, Washington, DC 20591; telephone: (202) 267-8783.

Raul Garza Jr., Federal Aviation Administration, Operations Support Group, Central Service Center, 10101 Hillwood Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76177; telephone (817) 222-5874.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it establishes Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Ranch at Double Gates Airport, Coleman, TX, to support IFR operations.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-9213 in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 51403; August 10, 2026) proposing to establish Class E airspace at Ranch at Double Gates Airport, Coleman, TX. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. No comments were received.
Incorporation by Reference
Class E airspace designations are published in paragraph 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO
( printed page 65681)
7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action modifies 14 CFR part 71 by establishing Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface within a 7.2-mile radius of Ranch at Double Gates Airport, Coleman, TX. This action is the result of instrument procedures being developed for this heliport to support IFR operations.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore: (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under Executive Order 12866; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Rulemaking and Guidance Procedure” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the controlled airspace. Since these amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this rule, when promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Environmental Review
The FAA has determined that this action qualifies for categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,” paragraph B-2.5(a), which categorically excludes from further environmental impact review rulemaking actions that designate or modify classes of airspace areas, airways, routes, and reporting points (see 14 CFR part 71, Designation of Class A, B, C, D, and E Airspace Areas; Air Traffic Service Routes; and Reporting Points); and paragraph B-2.5(k), which categorically excludes from further environmental impact review the publication of existing air traffic control procedures that do not essentially change existing tracks, create new tracks, change altitude, or change concentration of aircraft on these tracks. Additionally, the FAA determined that this action is not expected to result in any potentially significant environmental impacts, and no extraordinary circumstances exist that warrant preparation of an environmental assessment.
